sections.h2: Where is Meridian, Mississippi, and what is it known for?
sections.html:
Meridian is the county seat of Lauderdale County in east central Mississippi, about 93 miles east of Jackson and 154 miles southwest of Birmingham. With 35,052 residents at the 2020 census, it is the eighth most populous city in the state and the principal city of the Meridian micropolitan area.

The city grew up where two railroads crossed. It was established in 1860 at the junction of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and the Southern Railway of Mississippi, and from 1890 to 1930 it was the largest city in Mississippi. Rail traffic, timber and cotton built the downtown, and many of the buildings from that period still stand.

The terrain is gently rolling, with small creeks running through town. Sowashee Creek crosses the southern part of the city, fed by Gallagher's Creek, and Loper's Creek runs through the far west. If your lot is near one of these creeks, it is worth checking drainage before you list.

sections.h2: Why does Meridian have so many historic houses?
sections.html:
The railroad boom left Meridian with nine historic districts on the National Register of Historic Places. Wealth from the "Golden Age" between about 1880 and 1910 paid for the Grand Opera House in 1890, two Carnegie libraries in 1913 and the Threefoot Building in 1929, along with many houses in Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Italianate and bungalow styles.

The districts include East End, Highlands, Merrehope, Mid-Town, Poplar Springs Road, West End and the downtown areas around Union Station. The Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission was created in 1979 to protect that character. If your house sits in or near one of these districts, check with city planning before you change windows, siding or rooflines, since a buyer will ask whether past work was approved.

Age cuts both ways. A 1920s house can have character that appeals to a retail buyer. It can also carry knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized plumbing and a failing foundation pier, and those repairs scare off buyers who rely on mortgages. That is one reason owners of older Meridian homes consider an as-is sale.

sections.h2: What does the economy mean for Meridian home sellers?
sections.html:
Meridian's economy rests on health care, the military, retail and manufacturing, and the mix keeps it from depending on any one employer. Ochsner Rush Health is the largest health care employer in the region with 2,465 people, followed by Anderson Regional Health System with 1,343 and East Mississippi State Hospital with 943, based on April 2020 figures.

Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field together provide more than 4,000 jobs. NAS Meridian trains naval pilots, and Key Field hosts the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard. Peavey Electronics, which has made guitars and amplifiers since 1965, is headquartered in the city. Other manufacturers include Avery Dennison, Bimbo Bakeries USA and Tower Automotive.

Jobs at a hospital or a military base can involve relocation on short notice. When an owner has to move quickly, a cash sale can fit the timeline, because it avoids waiting on a buyer's loan approval.

  • Health care: Ochsner Rush Health, Anderson Regional, East Mississippi State Hospital.
  • Military: Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field.
  • Manufacturing: Peavey Electronics and several plants in four industrial parks.
  • Education: Meridian Community College and the Meridian Public School District.

sections.h2: How do roads, rail and air service affect a Meridian sale?
sections.html:
Meridian is connected by Interstate 20 and Interstate 59, which join in the city. Amtrak's Crescent stops at Union Station, a rebuilt 1906 design at 1901 Front Street, and Meridian Regional Airport at Key Field offers daily flights to Dallas/Fort Worth.

The airport's 10,004 foot runway is the longest public runway in Mississippi. The field sits about 3 miles southwest of the city, and a railroad line still runs through downtown, so location relative to the airport and the tracks is something a buyer may ask about.

sections.h2: What are the code rules for a vacant or run-down house in Meridian?
sections.html:
Meridian's Code Enforcement Division enforces city codes on property safety and maintenance, with four code officials assigned across the wards. Its list of possible violations includes abandoned or deteriorated structures, rubbish in the yard, inoperable vehicles, overgrown grass and weeds, appliances stored outdoors and fallen fences.

The city describes a clear sequence. An inspection happens, a notice of violation is issued if a violation exists, and a reinspection follows after a reasonable time. If the property is still out of compliance, a citation is issued and an environmental court appearance is scheduled. Fines or liens could follow.

A lien is something a buyer's title search will find. State law also lets a Mississippi municipality declare a property a menace and charge cleanup costs to the owner as an assessment against the land, under Mississippi Code section 21-19-11. If you inherited a Meridian house you have not visited in months, drive by and check for notices.

The city's code enforcement office is at 601-485-1998. Its page also links to the Secretary of State's list of tax-forfeited lands and to a neighborhood lot program, both of which show how vacant lots change hands in Meridian.

sections.h2: How does Lauderdale County property tax work for a seller?
sections.html:
Lauderdale County bills the tax, and it is due by February 1 following the January 1 assessment. Mississippi's Department of Revenue notes that bills are issued in November or December, and that taxes go to the county tax collector. The county's tax collector can be reached at 601-482-9895 for property tax questions.

A house in Meridian is subject to a county rate, a school district rate and a city rate. The state says an owner-occupied single-family home is assessed at 10 percent of value, while other real property is assessed at 15 percent. The county revalues real property at least once every four years, and interior inspections are not required.

If a bill goes unpaid, penalties and interest accrue. Eventually the property can be sold at the county tax sale, held either on the first Monday in April or the last Monday in August depending on the county. A lot that does not sell goes to the State of Mississippi and is managed by the Secretary of State. Clearing back taxes before closing keeps this problem off your sale.

An owner who disagrees with a valuation can ask for a Board of Supervisors hearing, usually by the first Monday in August before the taxes are due. Start with the chancery clerk.

sections.h2: What are your options for selling a house in Meridian?
sections.html:
Meridian sellers can list with an agent, sell privately, or accept a cash offer. Listing tends to suit a house in good condition in a stable neighborhood. A private sale saves a commission but leaves the disclosure form, contract and closing coordination with you.

Mississippi law requires the seller to deliver the written property condition disclosure statement as soon as practicable before title transfers (Mississippi Code section 89-1-503). A cash buyer still wants honest answers about the roof, plumbing, termite history and flooding.

The 2020 census count shows 13.6 percent of Meridian's housing units vacant, so a house in poor condition may compete with other empty homes. Owners of inherited, tenant-occupied or storm-damaged houses sometimes prefer a quick as-is sale over carrying taxes and insurance. We can look at your address and explain a no-obligation cash offer.

faqs.a: Meridian had 35,052 residents at the 2020 census and covers about 54.5 square miles. It is the eighth largest city in Mississippi and the seat of Lauderdale County.

faqs.q: When are Lauderdale County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Property taxes are due by February 1 of the year after the January 1 assessment. The tax collector's property tax line is 601-482-9895, and you can also pay online through the county's payment link.

faqs.q: Does Meridian have historic districts that affect my house?
faqs.a: Yes. Meridian has nine historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and a Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission created in 1979. Check with city planning before exterior changes in or near a district.

faqs.q: What happens if my Meridian house has a code violation?
faqs.a: The city inspects, issues a notice of violation, and reinspects after a reasonable time. If the problem persists, a citation is issued and an environmental court date is set. Fines or liens may result.

faqs.q: Do I need to give buyers a disclosure statement in Mississippi?
faqs.a: In most sales, yes. Mississippi Code section 89-1-503 requires the seller to deliver a written property condition disclosure statement as soon as practicable before transfer of title.

faqs.q: What is the climate like in Meridian, and does it matter for a house?
faqs.a: Meridian has a humid subtropical climate with about 58.65 inches of rain a year, and March is the wettest month. Severe thunderstorms can bring damaging wind, hail and tornadoes, most often in spring, so buyers look closely at roofs.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Meridian house that needs major repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer will usually purchase a house as-is. Be ready to disclose known defects, and clear any code liens or back taxes before closing.
